articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Superman’s Rachel Brosnahan Reveals Her Family’s Hilarious Thanksgiving Tradition—And What She Hopes Is Next for Lois Lane
articles.content: Rachel Brosnahan knows a thing or two about playing strong, outspoken women. After winning an Emmy and two Golden Globes for her role as the quick-witted Midge Maisel in The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, the actress traded stand-up comedy for superhero action, taking on the iconic role of Lois Lane in 2025’s Superman. And while she can certainly hold her own alongside the Man of Steel, Brosnahan has plenty of other things keeping her busy off-screen, especially with the holiday season right around the corner. In an exclusive interview with Reader’s Digest, Brosnahan gave us a peek into how she gets ready for the holidays, as well as the family traditions she looks forward to every year. She also revealed which of her famous on-screen characters she thinks would cause the most chaos at a holiday dinner party. (Spoiler alert: Midge Maisel would definitely keep things interesting.) But don’t worry, Superman fans: We didn’t forget about Lois Lane! Brosnahan also shared what it’s really like working with David Corenswet and what she hopes is next for her character in Man of Tomorrow, which hits theaters on July 9. And trust us—you’ll definitely want to hear what she has to say. Read to find out that and more. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long. This interview took place on Oct. 27, 2026, and has been edited for length and clarity. Reader’s Digest: You’ve played so many memorable characters, from Midge Maisel to Lois Lane. If you could invite three characters you’ve portrayed to a holiday dinner, who would make the guest list, and who would bring the most drama? Rachel Brosnahan: Midge Maisel would bring the most drama for sure. She could come. She’d keep us all entertained. I would also invite Lois Lane. I feel like she would be very practical, and she’d make sure that we had everything we needed. I play a character named Eve in a film that will likely come out sometime next year called Saturn Return. I would invite her because she’s a deeply soulful person who I feel would bring some kind of conversation starter game and really bring the heart to the gathering. Reader’s Digest: You’ve partnered with Ferrero Rocher to celebrate the holidays and the brand’s new limited-edition cinnamon spice chocolate squares. What drew you to the collaboration, and how does its message connect with the way that you personally celebrate this festive season? Rachel Brosnahan: The holidays are made by the people that you spend it with. For me, I love the holidays. It’s my favorite time of year, and it’s such a wonderful opportunity to slow down and just spend quality time with friends and family, with your neighbors. And I feel like it’s the only time we ever get to all slow down together at the same time, and so I’m so grateful for that part of it. I’ve also been such a fan of Rocher for a long time. My dad used to bring back the trays of pralines from business trips, and they made me feel very fancy. It was a year-round thing in our household, not just for the holidays. But I have such fond memories of that particular flavor, and it’s been really fun to get to try some new ones that I hadn’t tried yet, like the new cinnamon flavors. I love dark chocolate, and it just feels like the holidays in a square. Reader’s Digest: I love how you talked about bringing the family together. Is there an unforgettable or hilarious moment from a holiday gathering that your family still talks about today? Rachel Brosnahan: I’ve been celebrating the holidays with my same group of extended family since I was a little kid, and it’s been such a beloved tradition. Thanksgiving is our holiday, so we’ve all grown up together and gone from being children to adults. Now we’re at a stage where everybody is of drinking age in the family, so we have started a beloved holiday tradition to find the drunkest cousin every Thanksgiving. Whoever ends up the drunkest cousin has to get up at the end of dinner and give a very heartfelt speech. Reader’s Digest: We’re so excited to see you return as Lois Lane in Man of Tomorrow. What is one thing about playing her that surprises you, and is there a side of Lois that you’re hoping to explore next? Rachel Brosnahan: I constantly get surprised when I get introduced, mostly by the fans, to different comics that I hadn’t seen before. I’m kind of a research nerd, and I did a a pretty extensive deep dive ahead of shooting the first film. But every so often, I’ll get tagged in something or DM’d a comic that I hadn’t seen before, and it’s just so fun to see different artists’ interpretations of the character and different adventures that she goes on. James Gunn, our wonderful writer and director, knows this, but I’m dying for Lois to fight some bad guys and do a little more flying—maybe in the next one. Reader’s Digest: What is it like working with your co-star David Corenswet, aka Superman? Rachel Brosnahan: He is one of the most incisive and smart actors I’ve ever had the privilege of working with. He really sees both the whole picture and also the tiniest detail at the same time, and he’s such a wonderful collaborator. This probably wouldn’t surprise people, but he’s an accent connoisseur. You can hear many different accents in a day coming from David. Reader’s Digest: For some people, The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel and Superman are comfort watches. Do you have a favorite comfort watch during Thanksgiving or Christmas? Rachel Brosnahan: I love the film Love Actually. We watch it every year. I also love Miracle on 42nd Street. The Holiday is another one! I love all the old holiday movies. We don’t have a physical TV in our apartment, so I miss being able to turn it on and let whatever movie is on play back-to-back for a week straight. It’s one of my favorite parts of the holidays that we’ve lost a bit in the digital age, but maybe we can recreate it in some way this year. Reader’s Digest: What’s an unpopular holiday opinion that you’re willing to defend, even if it might cause an argument at the dinner table? Rachel Brosnahan: I think my unpopular holiday opinion is that you can cancel your attendance to a holiday party last minute. It’s a crazy time for people. People are navigating so many different things, and I feel like people get very sensitive about last-minute cancellations to holiday parties. Reader’s Digest: If your family and your closest friends were asked to reveal one thing about you that would completely surprise your fans, what do you think they would say? Rachel Brosnahan: This is not new information, but it’s the first thing that comes to mind because I feel like people keep getting surprised by it. Before I ran around in skirts for a living, I was an athlete, and I was on my high school wrestling team. That remains a fairly surprising fact. Reader’s Digest: As you head into the new year, what are you most looking forward to? Rachel Brosnahan: I’m sitting on so many secret updates that I can’t yet share, but I have a number of different projects that will become clearer toward the end of this year and into early next year. I’m also looking forward to the holidays this year as an opportunity to slow down, catch my breath and reconnect with people. Reader’s Digest: Dogs or cats? Rachel Brosnahan: Dogs. Reader’s Digest: Mornings or nights? Rachel Brosnahan: Nights. Reader’s Digest: What’s your favorite book? Rachel Brosnahan: Right now, it’s Joan Didion’s The Year of Magical Thinking. Reader’s Digest: What advice would you give to your younger self? Rachel Brosnahan: Invest in Microsoft. Reader’s Digest: Would you rather travel to the past or the future? Rachel Brosnahan: The past. Reader’s Digest: If you weren’t an actress, what would you be doing? Rachel Brosnahan: I think I’d be a teacher of some kind for first-graders. *Editor’s note: Reader’s Digest does not endorse any specific products or services. articles.title: Here’s Why Paper Towels Have Those Weird Patterns on Them—It’s Not Just for Looks!
articles.content:
When I steer my cart down the paper-towel aisle at the grocery store or Target, I immediately gravitate toward my favorite brand. My wife, on the other hand, seems to just grab any old thing that crosses her field of vision—which drives me crazy and is why I prefer to do the shopping whenever possible. It might sound silly, but we all have our go-tos.
In my wife’s defense, paper towels are pretty similar. Sure, some brands are stronger, thicker or use recycled paper, while others tout their innovative perforation options. But the overall concept—a quick, clean, disposable towel that’s always at the ready—spans brands and price ranges. Of course, there is one easy way to tell paper towels apart: the pattern that’s embossed on the paper.
Why do paper towels even have these patterns? They are pretty, and if you keep your paper towels on the counter, picking based on aesthetics makes sense. As long as they do the job, that is. Ahead, Jerry Ballas, who holds several patents for nonwoven paper innovations and currently serves on the board of directors for Sellars Absorbent Materials, maker of Bravo paper towels, explains what these patterns do and how they evolved.
Read on to learn all the insider info—including whether a specific type of pattern just might be superior to the rest.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, cleaning, entertainment, tech and travel all week long.
The first paper towels hit the market more than a century ago. Here’s the story: Back in 1879 Philadelphia, two brothers named Scott started a paper-goods company, soon developing toilet paper on a roll, a major innovation at the time. “They expanded to paper towels around 1910, when they began selling Sani Towels and, eventually, Scott Towels,” Ballas says. (Yep, the same Scott Towels you can still buy today!)
“They advertised the benefits of paper towels for hygiene, convenience, utility—strong when wet, good at wiping and picking up spills—and the fact that they were disposable,” Ballas says. Advertising ultimately became a key strategy for the Scott Paper Company, according to the City University of New York, and it was one of the first American companies to lean hard into marketing and branding.
No, but it didn’t take long for the idea to catch on. “Paper towels began to be embossed in the early 1920s as a quality improvement innovation,” Ballas says. “Embossing increased liquid holding capacity and made the product thicker and softer.”
Unfortunately, embossing also made the towel somewhat weaker, so manufacturers tried to optimize the benefits while minimizing strength loss. “This was at a time when paper towels were a single-ply paper web,” Ballas says. “The embossing pattern was a very tight pattern and not highly aesthetic.”
But as the industry evolved, so did the embossing. “Around the early 1950s, a two-ply paper towel was developed that required embossing and laminating to create a pattern on the paper towel and hold the 2-plies together,” Ballas says.
It’s not just for looks … but that is a factor. At its heart, though, embossing is all about function, from how much liquid that unassuming paper towel will hold to how strong it is. Here’s the lowdown, along with some interesting facts about this household staple.
Embossing a pattern on paper towels creates pockets between the two plies of paper, which significantly increases their water-holding capacity, Ballas says. This is done through a high-pressure forming process that raises a pattern above the surface of the paper, giving it a three-dimensional effect and allowing it to absorb more liquid.
Raising a pattern on the surface makes the paper towel thicker, which contributes to a softer, squishier feel. But this also adds bulk, which despite sounding great for a towel designed to pick up spills, can cause performance to suffer. That’s because embossing can diminish the wet strength of a paper towel, which is not ideal for a product designed to be used when wet.
Ballas actually helped develop a technology called double re-creping (DRC) to tackle just this issue. The DRC technique creates a textured surface on single-ply towels, improving wet strength and reducing bulk while maintaining a softer, cloth-like feel.
Not many people want to use a kitchen paper towel that looks like it would also be at home in a gas station bathroom. So, yes, there’s also an aesthetic reason for embossing patterns on paper towels, notes Ballas. Specific patterns also make brands stand out: In a 2012 patent application for a specific embossing technique, Proctor & Gamble cited paper-product patterns as one way for manufacturers to distinguish themselves.
Embossing under high pressure also keeps the two plies of a two-ply paper towel together. That said, embossing isn’t the only way to do this; plies can also be joined through lamination, which is more like gluing, or the two processes can be combined.
Besides wanting to stand out from other paper products, manufacturers spend a lot of time and resources figuring out which patterns work best for their particular needs.
“Designs are developed and evaluated in laboratory form to define the overall results,” Ballas says. “In the end, the paper manufacturer makes the decision on the pattern chosen based on the overall benefits the pattern will deliver.”
The manufacturing techniques and scientific findings regarding TP’s patterns are pretty similar to those of paper towels. There’s one big difference, though: wet strength. Toilet paper is designed to break up quickly after use so it doesn’t clog your toilet or stick around in city wastewater-treatment facilities or your septic system.
It’s hard to definitively say which pattern is best. One study in Polymers found that micropatterns (smaller, denser patterns like dots) created more bulk and that more pronounced embossing reduced wet strength slightly. But researchers say the strength reduction was within the standard deviation. Translation: It was minimal.
Ballas says a quality paper towel comes down to a few things: strength when wet, liquid capacity and a low-lint, towel-like softness that wipes dry. But it’s hard to tell these things without trying them out.
So in the end, it mostly boils down to personal preference and experience. When I steer my cart toward my favorite paper towels, it’s because I like them enough to buy them again and again. They pick up spills, they don’t disintegrate in my hands and they don’t cost an arm and a leg. In other words, I have brand loyalty, which is something companies spend a lot of money cultivating.

articles.title: These Scams Fooled Real People—Could They Fool You Too?
articles.content:
You’d never fall for a scam, right? You know better than to send money to a mysterious prince (or princess), click a link promising you’ve won a vacation you never entered, or hand over your password to a stranger. Easy enough. Except today’s scams aren’t always that obvious. Some look, sound and feel so convincing that even the savviest among us could be fooled, and by the time you realize something’s off, the scammer may already have what they came for.
That’s why we’re sharing true stories of the sneakiest scams that tricked people—and could lure you in too if you don’t know what to look for. We’ll tell you what happened, highlight the red flags they missed and note the steps you can take to protect yourself in a similar situation.
Read on for the real-life scams that seem surprisingly legit, plus how to spot them before you become a cautionary tale for someone else.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, scams, history, cleaning, travel and fun facts all week long.
It was a sultry July day in 2025, and Christine, 86, was enjoying the air conditioning in her Philadelphia home, surrounded by photographs of her loved ones. When the phone rang, displaying a number she didn’t recognize, she answered and heard a sound no grandparent should ever be subjected to: her granddaughter’s sobs.
“What’s the matter, hon?” Christine asked. Her anguished “granddaughter,” according to NBC10, replied that she’d been injured in a car crash and was being detained by police. Before Christine could fully process the horrifying news, a new speaker joined the conversation, introducing himself as “John,” her granddaughter’s lawyer. He said he needed $10,400 to get her granddaughter out of jail. Christine said she only had $6,000 on hand in cash. That would have to do, said John. He told her he would send a car over immediately to pick it up, then kept her on the phone while another man arrived a little later for the money.
Minutes after that man left with the cash in hand, Christine’s grandson, who lives next door, showed up at her house. That’s when she learned the good news: Her granddaughter was, in fact, fine. She also learned some bad news: She had just become another victim of AI-assisted voice cloning.
Not so long ago, it was easier to spot scammers by their voices. If they sounded like impostors or recordings, you could simply hang up the phone and go about your day. Not anymore. With just a few recorded words, scammers can use AI to replicate someone’s voice and convince even family members that a loved one is in danger. The process is called voice cloning, and it’s frighteningly simple. As Christine’s granddaughter told NBC10, “It’s not hard to find something of my voice. I’m on social media.”
To protect against this, NBC recommends that you choose a security word with your family or that you ask whomever you’re talking to a question that “only a family member would know the answer to.” If that person doesn’t respond correctly, you might be talking to someone else.
If the voice on the line tells you to go buy an app or a gift card or wants payment in cryptocurrency, hang up immediately. Scammers are partial to crypto because transactions are quick, irreversible and lack the built-in protections offered by banks.
You can protect your own identity by staying quiet whenever taking suspicious or unsolicited phone calls. Don’t bother saying “Hello” (which confirms your number as active). And don’t ask to be removed from call lists, as even 10 seconds of audio may be all that the scammers need to con your family.
In an era of disinformation, stolen valor is a particularly odious scam. It’s what happens when someone lies about or misrepresents their military service to garner respect or other benefits reserved for actual heroes. Just last year, MPR News reported that a Minnesota man had been convicted of passing himself off as a wounded Marine and prisoner of war to garner over $100,000 in benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Stolen valor is not new. Among the most famous cases is one involving Jackie Stern, who wove a web of lies that began soon after he moved to Fort Lauderdale, Florida, from the New York City area in 1989. His former neighbor Alberto Lopez told the Tampa Bay Times that Stern let everyone know he’d been a Purple Heart recipient and a POW during the Korean conflict. “Out of respect for the guy, you let him talk,” said Lopez.
Stern spun his yarns and eventually greeted veterans returning home from the Gulf War in 1991 while wearing the Congressional Medal of Honor, the highest military decoration awarded by the United States. Stern claimed he’d received it for heroism. In reality, the award had been an unauthorized medal that Stern had purchased for $500 at a military memorabilia show in New Jersey, the Orlando Sentinel reported.
Stern’s lies knew no bounds. He even bragged to Broward County detectives that he’d been a New York City police detective, although he was actually a truck driver. That may have been his undoing. Detective Sgt. Daniel Ciacciarelli received a tip about a Medal of Honor stolen from the New York City area around the time Stern had arrived in Florida. Having always thought Stern was a bit of a blowhard, he checked with the Congressional Medal of Honor Society and learned there was no record of Stern receiving the honor. The detective concocted a plan. He tricked Stern into coming down to the station to pose for photographs with the medal, where he was arrested by a waiting FBI agent. It turned out that Stern, although he had served in the military, had never seen a day of combat.
For wearing an unearned military decoration and illegally modifying his official record with the Army, Stern was fined $250 and sentenced to a year on probation and 250 hours of community service at a Veterans Administration hospital. He also had to print an apology in his local newspaper for Memorial Day and—most creatively—write letters of apology to all 171 living Medal of Honor recipients at the time.
Stern admitted to the court that his goal was “personal and selfish,” reported the Orlando Sentinel, and added that he had wanted his children “to believe their father was a hero.”
According to USAMM.com, a veteran-owned retailer specializing in military medals and gear, indicators that point toward unearned medals include errors on the fraudster’s uniform, stories that don’t add up, over-the-top tales and a lack of knowledge of basic military jargon.
The National Archives cautions that lying about one’s military service is not necessarily illegal. It’s only a crime if someone lies about receiving certain medals to “obtain money, property or some other tangible benefit.” However, attempting to support these lies through forged documents, as Stern did, will likely violate separate laws.
Santiago Machado could not believe what he was hearing: a weeklong stay at the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic, for him and his extended family, for only $6,000—flights and three rooms included.
Machado, from South Florida, might have declined such telephone offers in the past, but this one sounded genuine. His friend enjoyed a Hard Rock membership, he told NBC Miami. Perhaps he had recommended Machado? The idea of a group vacation also hooked him. His mother in Cuba had never boarded an airplane before. What a nice surprise this would make!
Machado shared the news with his family and friends. Shortly after, they, too, were sending money and passport information to so-called representatives of the hotel. They were all set to go. But when some of Machado’s friends tried to change their arrival times, they found that no one at the hotel or the airline had any record of their reservations.
Outraged, Machado tried contacting the people who had sold him the package. But when he finally got through, “they were laughing,” he said.
Machado was out the $6,000. But there was also a new risk of identity theft since their personal information, passports and pictures had been shared as well. If that wasn’t enough, he now had to tell his mother and other family members in Cuba that the vacation was off. “[They all] cried when we told them … that it was all a scam and that we had lost the money,” Machado told Telemundo 51.
Machado’s first mistake was being too trusting. As the saying goes, if it looks too good to be true, chances are it is. In this case, looking online reveals that three rooms for three days at the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Punta Cana alone—without airfare—could run close to $6,000. Aside from an oddly cheap price, any typos or peculiar word choices in your exchanges with the “owners” should also make you think twice. Legit operations tend to know how to spell.
Before you put down a deposit, Navy Federal Credit Union suggests you make sure the hotel or vacation rental actually exists. You can do that by looking it up using Google Maps Street View and checking whether the property matches the picture in the listing, and by calling the front desk to verify the information if it’s a resort or hotel.
And never pay for a vacation rental by wire transfer, prepaid card, gift cards or apps like Venmo, as these payment methods aren’t easily reversible. Instead, Better Business Bureau spokesperson Cinthya Lavin told NBC Miami, pay with a credit card, which offers some protections.
Jeanette Voss, a retiree in Vermont, had her 2021 Memorial Day Weekend all planned out. And part of it would be spent watching a movie on her laptop. However, halfway into the film, a “screaming noise” blared from her computer, and then a pop-up filled the screen. The message was clear enough, she told AARP: “Call Microsoft. Call Microsoft.”
Voss picked up her phone and called the number on the screen, assuming she’d be connected to a Microsoft specialist. After getting the noise to stop, the “specialist” passed Voss on to more specialists, one supposedly from her financial institution. Yet another came on and told her, “We can see where you made a gambling bet of $213,000.”
“I most certainly did not,” she replied. She then heard those words that you never want to hear in the same sentence: hackers and Social Security number. Voss’s movie night was ruined.
The man explained they would need to transfer all her assets into a “secure digital wallet” for safekeeping, she told Seven Days, a Vermont newspaper. In the meantime, the man warned, “trust no one.” Jeanette agreed, and over the next six months she spoke repeatedly to two men, using a prepaid cellphone because hers was “compromised.”
All of Voss’s assets, including retirement savings and stocks that she had carefully managed for years, were moved with her assistance into online accounts and cryptocurrency wallets that totaled nearly $950,000. And then the conversations ended and the money was gone.The loss was life-changing, forcing Voss to completely alter her spending habits. All she had to live on were her monthly Social Security checks, which were barely enough to make ends meet. She cut back on groceries, unplugged devices when she wasn’t using them and had to miss a funeral because of travel costs. She became isolated, spending her days just with the birds and squirrels outside her door. Her life, she told Seven Days, was one of “unrelenting stress.”
But then, a miracle. Four and a half years later, in December 2025, Voss found out that Secret Service agents had traced her funds to a cryptocurrency account associated with a man involved in an international scam ring, Vermont Public Radio reported: “After seizing the crypto wallet, government officials sold the tokens in order to compensate Voss.” It was a rare victory for the good guys against the dark web. To celebrate, Voss bought groceries for herself, and for the birds and squirrels that “kept me sane.”
The fake alert that so alarmed Voss was likely accidentally downloaded days or even weeks earlier when she clicked on an ad in, say, Facebook, Doug Shadel, a fraud expert, told Seven Days. When “this pop-up occurs with a phone number to call and sirens going off, you call the number because you’re panicked,” he explained. If this should happen to you, Microsoft says to immediately close your browser. If it won’t close, restart your computer.
Still unnerved? Keep in mind that tech companies like Microsoft usually direct users to official websites and support pages, never to phone numbers provided in pop-up windows. Also, no major computer company will ever request that you pay them via cryptocurrency or gift cards.
And always remember: While there are some wonderful things about the internet (funny beagle videos, obviously!), there are also questionable characters lurking about waiting for you to inadvertently hit the wrong link. So be skeptical if someone asks for personal information or offers you a deal that’s too good to be true. It probably is.

Minutes after that man left with the cash in hand, Christine’s grandson, who lives next door, showed up at her house. That’s when she learned the good news: Her granddaughter was, in fact, fine. She also learned some bad news: She had just become another victim of AI-assisted voice cloning.

How to spot it

Not so long ago, it was easier to spot scammers by their voices. If they sounded like impostors or recordings, you could simply hang up the phone and go about your day. Not anymore. With just a few recorded words, scammers can use AI to replicate someone’s voice and convince even family members that a loved one is in danger. The process is called voice cloning, and it’s frighteningly simple. As Christine’s granddaughter told NBC10, “It’s not hard to find something of my voice. I’m on social media.”

To protect against this, NBC recommends that you choose a security word with your family or that you ask whomever you’re talking to a question that “only a family member would know the answer to.” If that person doesn’t respond correctly, you might be talking to someone else.

If the voice on the line tells you to go buy an app or a gift card or wants payment in cryptocurrency, hang up immediately. Scammers are partial to crypto because transactions are quick, irreversible and lack the built-in protections offered by banks.

You can protect your own identity by staying quiet whenever taking suspicious or unsolicited phone calls. Don’t bother saying “Hello” (which confirms your number as active). And don’t ask to be removed from call lists, as even 10 seconds of audio may be all that the scammers need to con your family.

Stolen-valor scam

The fake-out

In an era of disinformation, stolen valor is a particularly odious scam. It’s what happens when someone lies about or misrepresents their military service to garner respect or other benefits reserved for actual heroes. Just last year, MPR News reported that a Minnesota man had been convicted of passing himself off as a wounded Marine and prisoner of war to garner over $100,000 in benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Stolen valor is not new. Among the most famous cases is one involving Jackie Stern, who wove a web of lies that began soon after he moved to Fort Lauderdale, Florida, from the New York City area in 1989. His former neighbor Alberto Lopez told the Tampa Bay Times that Stern let everyone know he’d been a Purple Heart recipient and a POW during the Korean conflict. “Out of respect for the guy, you let him talk,” said Lopez.

Stern spun his yarns and eventually greeted veterans returning home from the Gulf War in 1991 while wearing the Congressional Medal of Honor, the highest military decoration awarded by the United States. Stern claimed he’d received it for heroism. In reality, the award had been an unauthorized medal that Stern had purchased for $500 at a military memorabilia show in New Jersey, the Orlando Sentinel reported.

Stern’s lies knew no bounds. He even bragged to Broward County detectives that he’d been a New York City police detective, although he was actually a truck driver. That may have been his undoing. Detective Sgt. Daniel Ciacciarelli received a tip about a Medal of Honor stolen from the New York City area around the time Stern had arrived in Florida. Having always thought Stern was a bit of a blowhard, he checked with the Congressional Medal of Honor Society and learned there was no record of Stern receiving the honor. The detective concocted a plan. He tricked Stern into coming down to the station to pose for photographs with the medal, where he was arrested by a waiting FBI agent. It turned out that Stern, although he had served in the military, had never seen a day of combat.

For wearing an unearned military decoration and illegally modifying his official record with the Army, Stern was fined $250 and sentenced to a year on probation and 250 hours of community service at a Veterans Administration hospital. He also had to print an apology in his local newspaper for Memorial Day and—most creatively—write letters of apology to all 171 living Medal of Honor recipients at the time.

Stern admitted to the court that his goal was “personal and selfish,” reported the Orlando Sentinel, and added that he had wanted his children “to believe their father was a hero.”

How to spot it

According to USAMM.com, a veteran-owned retailer specializing in military medals and gear, indicators that point toward unearned medals include errors on the fraudster’s uniform, stories that don’t add up, over-the-top tales and a lack of knowledge of basic military jargon.

The National Archives cautions that lying about one’s military service is not necessarily illegal. It’s only a crime if someone lies about receiving certain medals to “obtain money, property or some other tangible benefit.” However, attempting to support these lies through forged documents, as Stern did, will likely violate separate laws.

Vacation scam

The fake-out

Santiago Machado could not believe what he was hearing: a weeklong stay at the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic, for him and his extended family, for only $6,000—flights and three rooms included.

Machado, from South Florida, might have declined such telephone offers in the past, but this one sounded genuine. His friend enjoyed a Hard Rock membership, he told NBC Miami. Perhaps he had recommended Machado? The idea of a group vacation also hooked him. His mother in Cuba had never boarded an airplane before. What a nice surprise this would make!

Machado shared the news with his family and friends. Shortly after, they, too, were sending money and passport information to so-called representatives of the hotel. They were all set to go. But when some of Machado’s friends tried to change their arrival times, they found that no one at the hotel or the airline had any record of their reservations.

Outraged, Machado tried contacting the people who had sold him the package. But when he finally got through, “they were laughing,” he said.

Machado was out the $6,000. But there was also a new risk of identity theft since their personal information, passports and pictures had been shared as well. If that wasn’t enough, he now had to tell his mother and other family members in Cuba that the vacation was off. “[They all] cried when we told them … that it was all a scam and that we had lost the money,” Machado told Telemundo 51.

How to spot it

Machado’s first mistake was being too trusting. As the saying goes, if it looks too good to be true, chances are it is. In this case, looking online reveals that three rooms for three days at the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Punta Cana alone—without airfare—could run close to $6,000. Aside from an oddly cheap price, any typos or peculiar word choices in your exchanges with the “owners” should also make you think twice. Legit operations tend to know how to spell.

Before you put down a deposit, Navy Federal Credit Union suggests you make sure the hotel or vacation rental actually exists. You can do that by looking it up using Google Maps Street View and checking whether the property matches the picture in the listing, and by calling the front desk to verify the information if it’s a resort or hotel.

And never pay for a vacation rental by wire transfer, prepaid card, gift cards or apps like Venmo, as these payment methods aren’t easily reversible. Instead, Better Business Bureau spokesperson Cinthya Lavin told NBC Miami, pay with a credit card, which offers some protections.

Tech-support scam

The fake-out

Jeanette Voss, a retiree in Vermont, had her 2021 Memorial Day Weekend all planned out. And part of it would be spent watching a movie on her laptop. However, halfway into the film, a “screaming noise” blared from her computer, and then a pop-up filled the screen. The message was clear enough, she told AARP: “Call Microsoft. Call Microsoft.”

Voss picked up her phone and called the number on the screen, assuming she’d be connected to a Microsoft specialist. After getting the noise to stop, the “specialist” passed Voss on to more specialists, one supposedly from her financial institution. Yet another came on and told her, “We can see where you made a gambling bet of $213,000.”

“I most certainly did not,” she replied. She then heard those words that you never want to hear in the same sentence: hackers and Social Security number. Voss’s movie night was ruined.

The man explained they would need to transfer all her assets into a “secure digital wallet” for safekeeping, she told Seven Days, a Vermont newspaper. In the meantime, the man warned, “trust no one.” Jeanette agreed, and over the next six months she spoke repeatedly to two men, using a prepaid cellphone because hers was “compromised.”

All of Voss’s assets, including retirement savings and stocks that she had carefully managed for years, were moved with her assistance into online accounts and cryptocurrency wallets that totaled nearly $950,000. And then the conversations ended and the money was gone.The loss was life-changing, forcing Voss to completely alter her spending habits. All she had to live on were her monthly Social Security checks, which were barely enough to make ends meet. She cut back on groceries, unplugged devices when she wasn’t using them and had to miss a funeral because of travel costs. She became isolated, spending her days just with the birds and squirrels outside her door. Her life, she told Seven Days, was one of “unrelenting stress.”

But then, a miracle. Four and a half years later, in December 2025, Voss found out that Secret Service agents had traced her funds to a cryptocurrency account associated with a man involved in an international scam ring, Vermont Public Radio reported: “After seizing the crypto wallet, government officials sold the tokens in order to compensate Voss.” It was a rare victory for the good guys against the dark web. To celebrate, Voss bought groceries for herself, and for the birds and squirrels that “kept me sane.”

How to spot it

The fake alert that so alarmed Voss was likely accidentally downloaded days or even weeks earlier when she clicked on an ad in, say, Facebook, Doug Shadel, a fraud expert, told Seven Days. When “this pop-up occurs with a phone number to call and sirens going off, you call the number because you’re panicked,” he explained. If this should happen to you, Microsoft says to immediately close your browser. If it won’t close, restart your computer.

Still unnerved? Keep in mind that tech companies like Microsoft usually direct users to official websites and support pages, never to phone numbers provided in pop-up windows. Also, no major computer company will ever request that you pay them via cryptocurrency or gift cards.

And always remember: While there are some wonderful things about the internet (funny beagle videos, obviously!), there are also questionable characters lurking about waiting for you to inadvertently hit the wrong link. So be skeptical if someone asks for personal information or offers you a deal that’s too good to be true. It probably is.
